title: Falling Objects with Drag and RC Circuits
short: Model velocity with air resistance and charging circuits.

blocks.html: Newton's second law for a falling object and Kirchhoff's voltage law for a simple circuit both produce the same kind of linear first-order equation, $y' + ay = b$. Learning to read that equation once pays off in both places.

$y' + ay = b$ with $a > 0$ has the equilibrium $y = \frac{b}{a}$, and every solution approaches it like $e^{-at}$: $$y = \frac{b}{a} + \left(y_0 - \frac{b}{a}\right)e^{-at}.$$ The time constant $\frac{1}{a}$ is the time to close about 63% of the remaining gap.

For the falling object, take down as positive. Gravity pulls down with force $mg$; air resistance $kv$ pushes against the motion. So $mv' = mg - kv$. As $v$ grows, the drag grows until it balances gravity at $v_T = \frac{mg}{k}$, the terminal velocity. In a circuit, the battery voltage $E$ equals the sum of the voltage drops: $Ri$ across a resistor, $\frac{q}{C}$ across a capacitor, $Li'$ across an inductor, with $i = q'$.

blocks.title: Terminal velocity
blocks.q: A 2 kg object falls from rest with drag $4v$ newtons ($g = 9.8$ m/s²). Find $v(t)$ and the time to reach half the terminal velocity.
blocks.a: $v = 4.9(1 - e^{-2t})$ m/s; half speed after $\frac{\ln 2}{2} \approx 0.35$ s

blocks.title: Charging a capacitor
blocks.q: An RC circuit has $R = 100$ Ω, $C = 0.001$ F and a 9 V battery; the capacitor starts uncharged. Find $q(t)$ and the current.
steps: Equilibrium $q = CE = 0.009$ C; time constant $RC = 0.1$ s.
blocks.a: $q = 0.009(1 - e^{-10t})$ C; the current starts at $\frac{E}{R} = 0.09$ A and dies away

blocks.title: Switching on an inductor
blocks.q: An RL circuit has $L = 0.5$ H, $R = 10$ Ω and $E = 12$ V, with $i(0) = 0$. Find $i(t)$.
steps: Steady current $\frac{E}{R} = 1.2$ A, time constant $\frac{L}{R} = 0.05$ s.

blocks.html: Sign errors in the force balance. Drag always opposes motion; with down positive it is $-kv$. If your terminal velocity comes out negative, or if the speed grows without limit, a sign is wrong. A second slip is forgetting to divide by $m$ (or $R$, or $L$) before reading off the rate $a$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Velocity of a falling object from rest, $v = \frac{mg}{k}(1 - e^{-kt/m})$, with its terminal velocity dashed. A heavier object or a smaller drag constant raises $v_T$ and also lengthens the time constant $\frac{m}{k}$.
